notes.claim: A three-phase generator has three coils of wire placed at 120 degrees to each other and rotated in a magnetic field.
The line voltage is found by taking the phasor sum of the voltages in two phases, which gives the factor root 3.
In balanced star circuits line voltage is root 3 times phase voltage and line current equals phase current; in balanced delta the roles reverse.
Three-phase power equals the product of line-to-line voltage, line current, root 3 and the power factor.
The neutral conductor carries no current in a balanced three-phase network.
Triplen harmonic currents add within the neutral of a 4-wire Y-Y system, so 'balanced means no neutral current' holds for sine-wave loads.
For i10: delta-connected sources are more reliable if a winding fails, while star-connected sources deliver the same power with less line current (explain paragraph 3 and the closing line).
For i10: most ships run a three-phase, three-wire 440 V system, so their main supply has no neutral conductor (SECONDARY; screen 2's and screen 4's Why? and explain paragraph 2).
For i10: a US Navy training problem has a 450 V three-phase system supplying a delta-connected 100 hp load at 0.92 lagging (explain paragraph 3).
For i10: UK mains is 230 V rms and peaks at about 325 V (230 times root 2), the rule screen 13 applies to a 400 V line voltage (practice).

sources.title: maritime electrical installations - notes on design ...
sources.quote: The majority of ships have a 3 phase, 3 wire, 440V insulated neutral system. This means that the neutral point of star connected generators is not earthed to the ship's hull. For Continental European vessels, a 380V, 3 phase system is common.

sources.quote: Δ-connected three-phase voltage sources give greater reliability in the event of winding failure than Y-connected sources. However, Y-connected sources can deliver the same amount of power with less line current than Δ-connected sources.
